rationale: Both express strenuous concern for the recipients and Laodicea. Here the speaker describes his struggle, including people who have not seen him; the closing reports Epaphras's great pains and also names Hierapolis. The workers and personal-contact statements remain distinct.

Both connect understanding with the mystery of Christ. Ephesians develops the revealed mystery through the nations' shared inheritance and body; Colossians names encouraged hearts, love and full assurance in knowing God's mystery—Christ. The actual title and syntax are preserved.

The treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden in Christ correspond to Christ called God's power and God's wisdom. The earlier letter contrasts hearers' reactions; it does not reproduce the full treasures-and-knowledge statement.

Both warn against deception through speech. Colossians names persuasive argument; Ephesians names empty words and connects them with disobedience and wrath. The warnings are related without identifying the same teachers.

Both contrast bodily absence with presence in spirit. Corinthians applies the formulation to a judgment about misconduct; Colossians joins it to rejoicing over order and firm faith. The differing purposes are kept.

Both connect what was received with the recipients' manner of walking. Colossians says they received Christ Jesus the Lord and should walk in Him; Thessalonians recalls instruction in walking to please God and urges further progress.

Both join rootedness with relation to Christ and faith. Ephesians describes Christ dwelling through faith and being rooted and founded in love; Colossians describes rootedness, building and established faith in Him with thanksgiving. The images and stated objects differ.

Both warn about subjection to the world's elements rather than the life associated with Christ or knowing God. Galatians asks about turning again to weak and poor elements; Colossians names human tradition and empty deceit. It does not identify every philosophical inquiry as the same teaching.

All fullness dwelling in Him repeats the earlier fullness-dwelling statement. This unit explicitly adds deity and bodily; the earlier statement says God was pleased that all fullness dwell in Him. The wording of neither is expanded to match the other.

Both connect Christ with supremacy over rulers and authorities and with fullness. Ephesians describes being above the powers and head over all things to the Church; Colossians describes recipients filled in Him as head of every ruler and authority.

Both contrast circumcision understood beyond an outward fleshly operation. Romans speaks of the heart, Spirit and letter; Colossians speaks of a circumcision not made by hands and the circumcision of Christ. Its body-of-flesh phrase is not expanded with an unprinted sins clause.

Both connect baptism with burial together with Christ and ensuing life or resurrection. Colossians explicitly names faith in God's working, who raised Him; Romans names the Father's glory and walking in newness of life. The formulations remain distinct.

Both describe people dead in transgressions being made alive with Christ. Ephesians develops the former course of life and God's mercy and grace; Colossians includes uncircumcision and forgiveness. Its change from you to us is preserved.

Both bring decrees, opposition or hostility, and the cross into their argument. Colossians speaks of wiping out an opposing handwritten record and nailing it to the cross; Ephesians speaks of abolishing the commandments-in-decrees law and reconciling both groups. The objects are not simply declared identical.

Both use a triumph image. Colossians describes rulers and authorities stripped and displayed openly, led in triumph in it; Corinthians thanks God who leads us in triumph in Christ. The different participants and prepositions remain as supplied.

Both address judgment involving food and observance of days. Romans distinguishes eaters and abstainers and varying regard for days; Colossians names eating, drinking, festivals, new moons and Sabbaths. No identical local dispute or weak-faith label is imposed.

Both use a shadow of things to come in discussing religious observance. Hebrews contrasts the law's shadow with the very image of realities; Colossians says the body belongs to Christ. Body is preserved rather than silently substituted with a different translation.

The later assessment again combines humility, worship practice and a flesh-related criticism. It evaluates a reputation for wisdom and severe bodily treatment; this unit also names angel worship and what someone has seen. The overlapping critique does not make every practice identical.

Both describe the body's growth through its relation to the head and its joined members. Ephesians explicitly names Christ as head and growth through each part in love; Colossians warns against failing to hold the head and names growth from God.

Both question renewed subjection to elements or religious regulations. Galatians speaks of returning to weak and poor elements and observing days and seasons; Colossians reasons from dying with Christ to why recipients submit to decrees as if still living in the world.

The following qualification locates the do-not-handle/taste/touch decrees among things perishing with use and human commandments and teachings. It supplies the explicit argumentative context, rather than treating the quoted prohibitions as new universal commands from the writer.

Both criticize teaching framed as human commandments. Matthew's saying concerns worship in vain while teaching human precepts; Colossians describes perishable things governed by human commandments and teachings. The settings and complete wording remain distinct.

The earlier warning also links humility and worship practice with fleshly inflation. The present assessment adds severe bodily treatment, a reputation for wisdom and lack of value against fleshly indulgence. The two parts of the critique are connected without changing their actual wording.
